title: Not Enough Rich Patients: Why Devi Shetty Built Narayana as a Business
dek: Around 2000 a Bangalore heart surgeon gave up on charity alone and set up a hospital company designed to make cardiac surgery cheaper through scale.

story.event: Founding a for-profit heart hospital in Bangalore, funded by his father-in-law, to cut the cost of cardiac surgery through scale
story.summary: Around 2000 the cardiac surgeon Devi Shetty, then running the Manipal Heart Foundation in Bangalore, concluded that letting paying patients subsidise poor ones could not reach enough people. With capital from his father-in-law, Charmakki Narayana Shetty, he set up Narayana Hrudayalaya as a for-profit company after finding a charitable trust could not raise enough, and built it around high volumes, surgical teams and daily cost tracking.
paragraphs: Devi Shetty came home from London in 1989 to set up a cardiac hospital in Calcutta, and later moved to Bangalore to build the Manipal Heart Foundation. In India, unlike in Britain, he met patients' families before and after surgery. Many people he saw needed an operation, which cost about Rs 1.5 lakh in the early 1990s, and never came back once they learned the price; they did not even ask for a discount, he later wrote. He had been letting patients who could pay subsidise those who could not. "I realised there weren't enough rich people who could subsidise the poor," he said.

His answer was a hospital of his own, built for volume. His brother-in-law persuaded Shetty's father-in-law, the construction businessman Charmakki Narayana Shetty, to put up capital so that the hospital would be his legacy, and it carries his name. Shetty first wanted a charitable trust, but found a trust could raise nowhere near enough, so Narayana Hrudayalaya was set up as a private company, incorporated in Bangalore on 19 July 2000. "Charity is not scalable but good business principles are," he said later.

The heart hospital opened in 2000 with about 225 beds, by Shetty's own count; Business Today, which dates the start to 2001, says 280. The model was volume: large hospitals and many patients, with surgeons working in teams so that a senior specialist did the critical grafting in a bypass while junior doctors opened and closed the chest. Patients who paid full price helped cover those who could not. At noon each day senior staff received a text with the previous day's revenue and costs, which told them how many free or subsidised operations they could accept.

Shetty later launched a five-rupees-a-month insurance plan for farmers that, he says, people laughed at. By 2014 the group had 26 hospitals and 6,900 beds, and its average bypass was put at about $1,500. He has said he still sees around 100 patients a day, and that he wishes he had spent more time with his family.

quote.text: sell not all thou hast, except thou come and follow me; that is, except thou have a vocation, wherein thou mayest do as much good, with little means as with great; for otherwise, in feeding the streams, thou driest the fountain.
quote.locator: Essay XIII, "Of Goodness and Goodness of Nature"
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Shetty found that a trust would run dry long before it reached enough patients, and chose a business that could keep paying for free operations. Bacon gives the same warning in older words: generosity that spends its own source soon helps no one.

reflection: It is easy to treat generosity and good business as opposites. Shetty's choice was to make the generosity depend on the business: a daily count of what came in, so that the hospital could keep saying yes to people who could not pay.

Bacon's fountain is not only an institution. It is also you: your sleep, your evenings, the people at home who carry what you leave undone. Shetty is frank that his family paid part of the cost of his work. Whatever you give at work, it is worth asking whether you could still give it in five years, and what would have to change for that to be true.
invitation: Pick one thing you regularly give away at work, whether an extra hour, a favour or a discount, and ask whether you could still afford it in five years. If not, change one small detail of how you give it.

sources.title: One Needs To Be Curious To Grow (Secret Diary of an Entrepreneur: Devi Prasad Shetty)
sources.supports: Shetty's first-person account: return from London in 1989 to set up the Birlas' cardiac hospital; moving to Bangalore to set up the Manipal Heart Foundation; meeting families in India; patients not returning after learning the cost and not asking for a discount; letting paying patients subsidise others; 'I realised there weren't enough rich people who could subsidise the poor'; his brother-in-law persuading his father-in-law, Charmakki Narayana Shetty, to provide capital; the 225-bed hospital of 2000 named after him; the shift from a charitable trust to a for-profit company; the Rs 5 a month insurance plan people laughed at; seeing about 100 patients a day; wishing he had spent more time with his family.

sources.title: Biggest Innovations: Narayana Health has successfully married affordability, quality health care
sources.supports: Cardiac surgery cost about Rs 1.50 lakh in the early 1990s and most patients never came back for it; founding in Bangalore dated to 2001; a 280-bed start; growth to 26 hospitals and 6,900 beds by 2014; average bypass cost of $1,500 (citing Vijay Govindarajan in HBR); surgical teams in which the specialist does the grafting and juniors the rest; the daily noon text of revenue, costs and EBITDA used to decide on free or subsidised surgery; micro-insurance schemes.

sources.title: Narayana Health: Providing world-class treatment to the poor (Forbes India Philanthropy Awards 2013)
sources.supports: Shetty's quotation 'Charity is not scalable but good business principles are'; cross-subsidy of non-paying patients by those who can pay; never refusing patients; daily knowledge of how many non-paying patients are being operated on; the Bangalore campus on Hosur Road.

cross_checks.claim: Shetty's father-in-law, Charmakki Narayana Shetty, provided the capital for the first Narayana hospital, which is named after him.
Narayana Hrudayalaya was incorporated and began operating in Bangalore in 2000 (Business Today gives 2001).
The decision rested on the view that charity could not scale and a business model could, with paying patients subsidising others.
Many patients who needed heart surgery never returned once they learned the cost.

research_notes: Founding date: the company was incorporated on 19 July 2000 and began operations in 2000 (Economic Times company history, from the company's filings), and Shetty himself dates the hospital to 2000; Business Today (2014) says 2001. The story uses 2000 and gives Business Today's date with attribution. Opening size: Shetty says 225 beds; Business Today says 280; both are given. Surgery cost abroad and at Narayana: Business Today cites Vijay Govindarajan's figure of $1,500 for an average bypass; Shetty told Forbes India in 2013 'cardiac surgery for $1,400'; the story uses $1,500 as 'put at about'. Share of India's heart surgeries: 12% (Business Today) vs 10% (Shetty to Forbes India); not used. Shetty's maxim appears in two wordings ('charity is not scalable while a sound business model is', Business Today; 'Charity is not scalable but good business principles are', Forbes India); the story quotes the Forbes India wording. Where he saw patients fail to return: Business Today places it at the Birla Heart Foundation in Kolkata in the early 1990s; Shetty's diary says simply 'in India'; the story keeps it general. The Magzter extract of Business Today's 'Building Trust' is cut off at the paywall and contains a confused line about a first hospital in Kolkata; it is cited only for the father-in-law's offer to fund. The farmers' insurance plan is described only as Shetty does (five rupees a month, laughed at); his claim that over 100,000 farmers had surgery under it is ambiguous in wording and not used. The HBS Working Knowledge piece and the Cureus profile (PMC) do not load for the verifier and are not cited. Bacon's 'vocation' line glosses the Gospel command to sell all and give to the poor; it is applied here to institutions and to the giver by analogy.
